newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen urges vote against Europe.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen urges vote against Europe.

text.p: French hard-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen on Monday portrayed his National Front party as a king-maker in a parliamentary election runoff, saying it would support candidates who endorsed its xenophobic programme.

"I issue an appeal to all candidates, and particularly to incumbents. I ask them to pledge, if they agree, if they are elected, to prevent France's submergence in the system of Maastricht," he said on RTL radio.

He said National Front support in next Sunday's poll also would be contingent on endorsement of the Front's plan to reserve jobs, housing, education, health care and welfare for native-born French citizens.

The National Front was basking in the political spotlight after scoring its best parliamentary election result in the first-round ballot on Sunday, and analysts agreed its supporters would probably determine whether the left or right would govern.
The Front boasted that its candidates would be standing in a stunning 133 of France's 577 constituencies in the second round.

Official Interior Ministry results gave the Front a national first-round score of 14.9 percent, only slightly less than the record 15 percent Le Pen won in the 1995 presidential election and significantly better than its 12.4 percent score in the last general election in 1993.

The ruling centre-right suffered a stinging rebuke from voters in the first round, setting the stage for a possible upset victory by an alliance of leftist parties including the Socialists and Communists.
Most importantly, polls showed that Front voters' choices in the runoff would probably decide the ultimate winner by swinging in greater numbers to either leftist or rightist candidates.

The Front, which advocates expelling three million immigrants, scored best in its traditional eastern and southern strongholds but also showed impressive gains in central France and some parts of suburban Paris.
Le Pen, who had reserved his harshest campaign attacks for Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, said on Sunday the first-round results meant the president should resign.

But on Monday he said the Front disliked both the right and the left and would therefore decide which non-Front candidates to support on a case-by-case basis, depending on their willingness to publicly declare their support for its goals.
He said he would announce which candidates had done so at a Paris rally on Thursday evening.
It was unlikely that any candidate would do so as mainstream politicians avoid any links to the far-right party.

The party's score was nonetheless an undeniable sign of its growing standing in France. Despite mainstream politicians' efforts to consign it to fringe status, the Front consistently enjoys the support of roughly one in every seven French voters.
CSA polling institute political director Roland Cayrol said the vote showed the Front was now a force to contend with in all French elections.

Tempering the Front's joy were pollsters' predictions that, despite its impressive share of the popular vote, it was likely to finish with just one member in the National Assembly, where it now has none. The most favourable projections gave it just three seats.
But Le Pen said the voter surveys were worthless and predicted his party would win as many as 20 seats in parliament.
